samples.text:
Today we can find international brands and fast-food restaurants almost in every country. This essay will explain why this has happened and how it affects local businesses and culture.

There are several reasons for this situation. Firstly, globalisation made trade between countries much easier than before. Many governments have reduced taxes on foreign companies, so big companies can open branches in other countries without many problems. Secondly, these brands are very popular, especially among young people, because they see them in films, on television and on the internet. For example, many teenagers want to eat in famous burger restaurants or wear sports shoes from well-known brands because they think it is modern and cool. Also, these companies have a lot of money for advertising, so they can attract customers everywhere.

This trend has some negative effects on local businesses and culture. International chains are usually cheaper and more famous, so small local shops and restaurants lose their customers and some of them have to close. For example, a family café may not survive when a big coffee chain opens on the same street. In addition, traditional food and clothes become less popular, especially with young generation, and every city starts to look the same with the same shops. However, there are also some positive effects. International companies create jobs for local people and they sometimes bring new ideas and higher standards of service which local businesses can learn.

In conclusion, international brands are everywhere because of globalisation, their popularity and strong advertising. Although they create jobs, I think they have a bad influence on small local business and traditional culture, so governments should protect them.
samples.why: Both questions answered with relevant points · effects discussed briefly and generally · repetitive vocabulary (companies, popular) · unclear reference in conclusion · errors in word order, articles and prepositions.

samples.text:
Global brands and fast-food chains have spread to almost every corner of the world, from major capital cities to small towns. This essay will discuss the reasons for this expansion and examine its effects on local businesses and culture, which I believe are largely negative.

The main reason for this spread is economic globalisation. Over recent decades, many countries have opened their markets to foreign investment and reduced trade barriers, making it far easier for multinational companies to operate abroad. Improvements in transport and communication have also allowed these companies to manage supply chains across continents. Another important factor is the power of global media. Through films, television and social media, consumers around the world are exposed to the same brands, which become associated with a modern, attractive lifestyle. As a result, a well-known coffee chain or clothing label can have instant appeal in a new market even before it opens its first store.

The effect on local businesses is often damaging. Multinational companies benefit from enormous marketing budgets and economies of scale, allowing them to offer lower prices and more consistent quality than small independent firms. Family-run cafés, restaurants and shops may therefore struggle to compete and eventually close down. Culturally, the growing dominance of global chains can weaken local traditions. When young people prefer international fast food to traditional dishes, or when high streets in different countries fill with identical shops, the distinctive character of a place begins to disappear. On the other hand, global brands does provide employment and sometimes encourage local firms to raise their standards, and some chains adapt their menus to local tastes.

In conclusion, international brands have spread because of open markets, better logistics and the influence of global media. While they create jobs, they often put pressure on local businesses and contribute to a loss of cultural diversity.
samples.why: Clear position on both questions with extended, relevant support · effective paragraphing and cohesion · good less common vocabulary (economies of scale, trade barriers) · frequent error-free sentences, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
From burger chains to coffee houses and sportswear labels, a handful of international brands have established a presence in almost every country on earth. Their spread is the product of economic liberalisation and global media, and its effects on local enterprises and cultural identity are, in my view, more harmful than beneficial, although not uniformly so.

The expansion has been driven above all by the opening of national markets. As governments have lowered trade barriers and actively courted foreign investment, multinational corporations have found it increasingly straightforward to establish outlets abroad, often through franchising arrangements that limit their financial risk. Advances in logistics mean that products can be sourced and distributed across continents with remarkable efficiency. Equally important is cultural reach. Films, television and social media have familiarised audiences everywhere with the same logos, and for many consumers, particularly the young, these brands carry an aura of modernity and cosmopolitan status long before a branch opens nearby.

For local businesses, the arrival of a global chain can be devastating. Such companies enjoy economies of scale, sophisticated marketing and the ability to absorb initial losses, advantages that independent restaurants and shops simply cannot match. Where these smaller enterprises close, profits that once circulated within the community are instead transferred abroad. The cultural consequences are subtler but equally significant. As international menus and products become the norm, traditional cuisine and crafts may come to seem old-fashioned, and town centres across the world grow increasingly indistinguishable. Nevertheless, the picture is not entirely bleak: multinationals provide employment and training, many adapt their offerings to local tastes, and competition can prompt local firms to differentiate themselves by emphasising authenticity.

In conclusion, global brands have proliferated because of open markets, efficient supply chains and the influence of global media. Although they bring jobs and some healthy competition, they frequently undermine independent businesses and erode the cultural distinctiveness that makes places unique.
samples.why: Both questions answered with a clear, qualified position · well-developed ideas in logical sequence · wide, sophisticated vocabulary (courted, franchising, indistinguishable) · wide range of structures with no errors.
